question: A 16-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 2-hour history of sudden-onset abdominal pain. He was playing football when his symptoms started. The patient’s past medical history is notable only for asthma. Social history is notable for unprotected sex with 4 women in the past month. His temperature is 99.3°F (37.4°C), blood pressure is 120/88 mmHg, pulse is 117/min, respirations are 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is noted for a non-tender abdomen. Testicular exam reveals a right testicle which is elevated with a horizontal lie and the scrotum is neither swollen nor discolored. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

paths: (Structure of right testis)-LOCATION_OF->(Pain in scrotum)-ASSOCIATED_WITH->(Spermatic Cord Torsion)
(Structure of right testis)-LOCATION_OF->(Pain in scrotum)-ASSOCIATED_WITH->(Spermatic Cord Torsion)

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Traumatic event during football game -> Right testicle elevated with horizontal lie -> Testicular torsion -> 80% CHAIN: Unprotected sex -> Possible sexually transmitted infection -> Epididymitis -> 70% CHAIN: Abdominal pain with non-tender abdomen -> Unlikely appendicitis -> Less likely to be appendicitis -> 60% CHAIN: Elevated right testicle with horizontal lie -> Testicular torsion more likely than other causes -> Testicular torsion -> 80%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the 16-year-old man presenting with sudden-onset abdominal pain and an elevated right testicle with a horizontal lie is testicular torsion. This is supported by the physical exam findings and the reasoning chain indicating a high likelihood of testicular torsion. The evidence paths linking the location of the right testis to spermatic cord torsion and ischemia further support this diagnosis.
analysis: The most likely diagnosis for the 16-year-old man with sudden-onset abdominal pain and an elevated right testicle with a horizontal lie is testicular torsion. The physical exam findings of an elevated testicle with a horizontal lie are classic for testicular torsion, a surgical emergency. This presentation is not consistent with appendicitis, epididymitis, seminoma, or traumatic urethral injury.
